items.question: Why did you see starting Mistral AI as a worthwhile opportunity despite the resources available to established AI companies?
items.object: The decision to start Mistral AI
items.answer: Guillaume and Timothée were, I guess, pretty early in the field, and it had been 10 years that we had been doing machine learning, and we did know where to start from and how to make a good model with a limited amount of compute and money. Well, not so limited, but at least more limited than where we were coming from. And so I think that's why we got it started. The various companies we were in moved into directions that we hadn't anticipated when we joined the company, and we decided that there would be a very good opportunity for creating something that would be a standalone company in Europe, focusing on making AI better, focusing on making frontier AI, and focusing on making open-source AI as a core value.

items.question: How did RETRO's use of external memory fit your approach to making language models more efficient?
items.object: RETRO and retrieval-augmented language models
items.answer: I come from an optimization background, so my focus has always been, for the last 10 years, to make algorithms more efficient and to use better the data that we have to make models with good prediction performance. At DeepMind, very quickly I started to work on retrieval-augmented models, with a paper called RETRO that I co-led with my friend Seb, who is still at DeepMind. The point there was to use very large databases during pre-training so that we didn't force knowledge into the model itself, and we would tell the model that it would have access to an external memory anyway. And so it was working quite well. We could actually lower the perplexity. That's what you work on when you make LLMs. There were some limitations that I think the community has started to address quite well, and that was at the time when retrieval methods weren't really mainstream. Now they've become completely mainstream.

items.question: How did you approach the mathematical problems involved in building and scaling sparse mixture-of-experts models?
items.object: Optimal transport and scaling laws for sparse mixture-of-experts models
items.answer: I worked on sparse mixture of experts also quite quickly. Optimal transport is a setting where you have, I guess, tokens; you need to assign them to devices, and you need to make sure that there's some good assignment in between the two of them so that the devices don't see too many tokens. And as it turns out, the way you do it is with optimal transport. Optimal transport is a mathematical framework to do it correctly. And so I started to work on introducing this to sparse mixture of experts, and very quickly we started to move on to scaling laws. How do you actually take the method that is working at a certain scale and try to predict how that will evolve with the scale, the number of experts, the amount of data you see? And so that's work I've done with many colleagues as well: how do you adapt the scaling law for dense models to a setting where you want to predict performance not only in relation to the size of the model, but also the number of experts?

items.question: Why do you consider Chinchilla a major paper in the history of large language models?
items.object: The Chinchilla paper and the balance between model size and training data
items.answer: I worked on Chinchilla, which is, I think, a major paper in the history of LLMs, also with Seb, Jordan, Lauren, and many other people. Basically, the story was that everybody was training models on too few tokens because of the paper from 2020 that happened to be not very well executed. What we observed is that you could actually correct that. Instead of training very large models on very few tokens, you should actually grow the number of tokens as you grow the size of the model, which, if you think about it, makes a lot of sense, because you don't want to have an infinite-size model looking at a finite number of tokens, and similarly you don't want to have a finite-size model looking at an infinite number of tokens.

items.question: Why do you think the Chinchilla scaling results were adopted so quickly?
items.object: Chinchilla scaling results
items.answer: That's something that we showed empirically, and I think that's something that was adopted very fast because it was a pure win. For the same amount of compute, you would get a model that would be better, but also a model that would be four times cheaper to serve. So that was definitely a gain.

items.question: What do you think Mistral 7B showed about the limits of model compression?
items.object: Mistral 7B and the limits of model compression
items.answer: As it turns out, we didn't go far enough. That's what we did at Mistral. We realized that there was also a lot of opportunity in actually compressing models more. I mean, we've seen with Llama that it was actually possible. What we showed with Mistral 7B is that we were definitely far away from the limit of compression. We somehow corrected that by making a model very, very small, super cheap to serve, super fast, running on your MacBook Pro, but still good enough to be useful. And so that's one of the first achievements we made in the company.

items.question: How do you think about balancing inference cost and training cost when building language models for a viable business?
items.object: The balance between inference cost and training cost in deployed language models
items.answer: So I think what we've seen in 2022, 2021, you had a few companies that were really focusing on pushing the performance of models. If you want to push the pure performance of models, you don't care about inference, because you're not going to use the model; you're just going to see whether they're good or not, and that's really for academic purposes. But then when you start thinking about deployment and enabling downstream applications, then you need to think about what it is going to cost in runtime. You're not only worried about the upfront payment you need to make to get the model, but you're also worried about the runtime. And so I think the coefficient that you put in between the inference cost and the training cost really is business-dependent. As a company that intends to have a valid business model, we think a lot about inference cost. We think that it's super important to get to a regime where inference is super cheap, so that you can run agents, you can use AI LLMs everywhere for all of your use cases, and you're not blocked by cost, which is the case for the largest model currently. So that's definitely something we had in mind, and we knew that we could make a model—a 7B, 7-billion-parameter model—very good. That's for sure.

items.question: Why do you see training larger language models as necessary even while pursuing strong small models at Mistral?
items.object: The role of larger language models in improving reasoning and smaller models
items.answer: It's definitely not the end of the story. Now the question is, do we train bigger models? And the answer is obviously yes. There's still a limit to what a certain model size can do. This limit was, I think, underestimated. But if you want to get to more reasoning capabilities, you do need to move into larger models. The other thing about moving into larger models is that it enables you to train smaller models that are better, through a variety of techniques like distillation or synthetic data generation. These two things are quite related. If you want to make very strong small models, you do need to have bigger models. And we are indeed training larger models, for sure.

items.question: How do you understand the role of openness in the rapid progress of machine learning before 2020?
items.object: Openness in machine-learning research before 2020
items.answer: If you look back at the history of machine learning in the last 10 years, it went very fast. I mean, we went from a poor cat-dog detector to something that basically looks human-intelligent, and it's useful to remember how that happened. It happened because you had many academic labs. You had many industrial labs actually spending more money on different problems, and there was full, almost full transparency until 2020. Whatever was done in whatever lab, even in a competing lab, was published at NeurIPS, was published at ICML, and every six months we would all gather and get new ideas. Ideas would circulate, and everybody would build on top of the work of others. That's the way we went from something potentially interesting to something very interesting.

items.question: Why do you see Mistral's commitment to openness as important at the current stage of AI development?
items.object: Mistral's commitment to open AI research
items.answer: Around 2020, some companies started to be quite ahead in some field and realized that some value could be accrued, and then, at that point, opacity made it back to the field. I think that's a cycle we've observed in software already, the cycle between openness and closeness. We are observing it again. We think that it's too early, and we think it's really damaging for science to actually move into such an opaque regime where you have a few companies basically doing the same thing, just not communicating about it, spending billions of compute doing exactly the same thing, and where really the technology we're looking at is not working completely yet. It still doesn't reason well. Memory mechanisms are not very well understood. Causality mechanisms are not well understood. It's not super steerable. There are a lot of biases. I mean, it's incomplete. There's many things to be done. We still need to invent new techniques. How are you going to invent new techniques if nobody is speaking about it, when in order to invent new techniques you still need to spend some large amount of money to actually try things that scale? And the few companies that have the money to spend have now refused to communicate. That's something that we deeply regretted, and that's something that we are trying to change, because we do have some substantial amount of money to actually spend on compute, we do have some good ideas, and we know that there's a big community that is awaiting for AI players, for open-source AI players, to appear. We're very grateful that Meta is moving in that direction. By doing what we do, by being much more open about the technology we create, we want to steer the community into a regime where things just work better, where things are safer because they're put under more scrutiny.

items.question: How do you approach safety policy for open-source large language models?
items.object: Safety policy for open-source large language models
items.answer: So I think we approach it from a very pragmatic point of view. The question is: is open-sourcing today a model that we do a dangerous thing? Is it actually enabling bad actors to misuse the model? Is it giving them extra marginal capacities in pursuing their bad endeavors? I think the answer to this question is no. That's my conclusion. We've seen a lot of ideas around bioweapons, around nuclear terrorism, and the like. It's very interesting because if you actually assume good faith of these arguments—and I think in many cases people are in good faith, and that's an assumption that we always make—and if you try to go down the arguments, we realized, as we did, that there was really nothing to it. Nothing is showing that an LLM is actually marginally better than a search engine to find knowledge on topics that would enable bad use. The other thing is that it's not even proven, and it's certainly very likely not to be the case, that knowledge is the bottleneck for the actual misuse we're talking about. You have two things: in order to demonstrate that open-sourcing large language models is actually unsafe, you need to demonstrate that they have marginal improvement over a web engine and that knowledge is the bottleneck for creation. In both cases, the answer to these two questions is no. And so that means that we believe that we can open-source models today, and that it's actually the best way of putting things under high scrutiny so that we are ready for potential new generations of models that could be superintelligent. In that case, I think we can revisit these premises. But today we're really talking about a compression of knowledge that is widely available on the web, and, marginally speaking, we're not creating anything that is more dangerous than before. So I think there's a trade-off, there's a dynamic conversation to be had. That's what we discussed at the AI Safety Summit. For sure this needs to be revisited as model capacities build. But today, banning open source and preventing it from happening is really a way to enforce regulatory capture. Even though the actors that would benefit from it don't want it to happen, by design, if you actually ban small actors from doing things in the most efficient way, which is open source, you do facilitate the life of the larger incumbents, and that's something that would be detrimental to Mistral's life, for sure.

items.question: How do you assess the proposed compute and scale thresholds for regulating AI models?
items.object: Proposed compute and scale thresholds for regulating AI models
items.answer: I don't exactly know how they came up with this threshold. It's a high threshold by any standard, because if you make the bad-faith assumption that this is the float 64, it actually gives you approximately 300 million last-run compute. That's high. That's not something we can even afford, and that we won't be able to afford for the coming years. It's very arbitrary, because who tells you that beyond that 10 to the 26 you end up with bad capacities? Models start to have the emergence of bad behaviors? That's definitely not proven. Relating capabilities to scale is also very approximate, in the sense that it really depends on the data. The data set is super important. I know there's a focus on bioweapons, so let's say if we want to prevent models from generating chemical compounds because we think it's an enabler of bad behaviors, which I said we don't think is the case, but if you do want to prevent that, you do need to adapt your compute FLOP budget to the data set that you're working on. As it turns out, that's what they did, because they actually made a specific FLOP budget for biology, I think. So you can see the bioweapon narrative building on. We should really focus on capabilities and not pre-market conditions. To some extent, there's still consensus around that. Everybody knows that it's imperfect, it's a proxy which is maybe fairly correlated, but definitely we need to come up with agreement on how we measure capabilities and on what capabilities we deem dangerous. I think we don't agree with one another on that topic, but these are really what should be the judge, and not obviously pre-market conditions or the number of FLOPs that you do.

items.question: How do you understand the way the AI bioweapon risk narrative gained traction among policymakers?
items.object: The emergence and amplification of the AI bioweapon risk narrative
items.answer: I think it's a very interesting question, and honestly I don't have the answer. It's almost epistemology at that point. How did this idea appear, and how did it get amplified by the policy people, and how did it actually end up being heard by national security? I think it started somehow by GPT-4 Annex D or something, on page 46. Not exactly the same numbers, but where they generated some chemical compound, and then they made a small remark saying, okay, maybe that's not the direction we want to take; we don't want to have a model that reasons about chemical compounds. The chemical compound in question wasn't dangerous, but it made this observation, which is definitely expected if you train on articles on biology. You're definitely going to be able to produce some chemical compounds. It's an expected observation. Somehow, people built things on top of it. Nothing was observed; no scientific studies in proper form were published. But then policy papers started to cite non-scientific papers, arguing that these were scientific evidences that the bioweapon narrative was actually true. Then policy papers started to cite the other policy papers, and all of a sudden you end up with 50 papers saying that for sure bioweapons are going to blow us up, and that this is what the policymakers read at the end. I think that's how we ended up where we are today. There's some deconstruction to be made, unfortunately. I think the open-source community hasn't been vocal enough because they didn't see it coming, but right now this is changing, and I'm very glad that it is.
quotes: I think it's a very interesting question, and honestly I don't have the answer. It's almost epistemology at that point. How did this idea appear, and how did it get amplified by the policy people, and how did it actually end up being heard by national security?

I think it started somehow by GPT-4 Annex D or something, on page 46. Not exactly the same numbers, but where they generated some chemical compound, and then they made a small remark saying, okay, maybe that's not the direction we want to take; we don't want to have a model that reasons about chemical compounds. The chemical compound in question wasn't dangerous, but it made this observation, which is definitely expected if you train on articles on biology. You're definitely going to be able to produce some chemical compounds. It's an expected observation.

Somehow, people built things on top of it. Nothing was observed; no scientific studies in proper form were published. But then policy papers started to cite non-scientific papers, arguing that these were scientific evidences that the bioweapon narrative was actually true. Then policy papers started to cite the other policy papers, and all of a sudden you end up with 50 papers saying that for sure bioweapons are going to blow us up, and that this is what the policymakers read at the end. I think that's how we ended up where we are today.

There's some deconstruction to be made, unfortunately. I think the open-source community hasn't been vocal enough because they didn't see it coming, but right now this is changing, and I'm very glad that it is.

items.question: How do you view the focus on AI as a potential cause of future pandemics in the wake of COVID-19?
items.object: The focus on AI-related pandemic risk after COVID-19
items.answer: The COVID trauma for sure played a role in that narrative. That's definitely a traumatism. Thirty million people died. That's definitely something we don't want to reoccur again. I don't think AI is going to be the one triggering the next pandemic. It's always going to be climate change. That's the way it was, and that's probably where the focus should be instead of focusing on hypothetical, non-proven biological risk in token generators.

items.question: How do you think guardrails for AI applications should be designed?
items.object: Modular guardrails for AI applications
items.answer: I think this is a very valid concern. Models can output any kind of text, and in many cases you don't want them to output any kind of text. When you build an application, you need to think about the guardrails you want to put on the model output, and potentially also on the input. You do need to have a system that filters input that are not valid, that you deem illegal, and output that are not valid or that you deem illegal. The way you do it, in our mind, is that you create a modular architecture that the application maker can use, which means you provide the raw model, so the model that hasn't been altered to ban some of its output space, and then you propose new filters on top of that that can detect output that we don't want. It can be pornography; it can be hateful speech, these things you want to ban when you have a chatbot, for instance. But these things you don't want to ban from the raw model, because if you want to use the raw model to do moderation, for instance, you want your model to know about this stuff. So really, assuming that the model should be well-behaved is, I think, a wrong assumption to make. You need to make the assumption that the model should know everything, and then on top of that have some modules that moderate and guide the model. That's the way we approach it, and it's a way of empowering the application maker in making a well-guarded application.

items.question: How do you think a healthy ecosystem for AI guardrail providers should work?
items.object: Competition and responsibility in AI guardrail provision
items.answer: We think it's our responsibility to make very good modules that allow guarding the model correctly. It's part of the platform, and we think it's the way—there should be healthy competition in that domain, with different startups working on guardrailing the models. The way you make this healthy competition is not by trusting a couple of companies to do their own safety. Rather, the way you do it is to ask application makers to comply with some rules, so chatbots should not output hateful speech.

items.question: How do you assess AI safety concerns ranging from harmful content and physical harm to existential risk?
items.object: AI safety risks: harmful content, physical harm, and existential risk
items.answer: So first of all, I think it's very important to address these three things separately, and to hammer home that our solutions exist for the first one; for the second one, there's no evidence that it actually exists at that point, and no evidence that it will exist in the near future. The third point, I think that's very philosophic. Obviously, if you can make a system of arbitrary complexity, it can start doing anything that you don't want it to do. We are not at a stage where the model has arbitrary complexity, and so this is very abstract to me. I think we'll move onto a world with agents and AI interacting with one another, and that will create a lot of complexity. Anticipating that complexity will necessarily yield to a collapse—we call it a collapse in machine learning when suddenly everything stops working because you fall into a local minima—well, it's unclear to me that complexity leads to a collapse. Usually complexity leads to doing nothing because there's no self-organization and no willpower to build something. So I'm not too worried about existential risk. Obviously this is a dynamic conversation. If we can make a model which is growingly intelligent, then maybe you're at a singularity level. There's no evidence whatsoever that we are on the way to doing that, to making that happen. So I think it's a very open conversation. I personally don't see the scientific evidence, and as a scientist I trust only what I can see.

items.question: What technological advances do you think would help make AI agents work better?
items.object: Smaller models and research needed to make AI agents work
items.answer: I think making a model smaller is definitely a way to make agents work, because one problem you have with agents is that very quickly, if you run an agent on GPT-4, you're going to run out of money. So if you divide by 100 the cost of compute, you can start to build more interesting things. What we see with agents is mode collapse, so not very interesting mode collapse. They start repeating themselves and they fall into loops. So definitely there's some research to be made there. There's some research to be made on making models more capable of reasoning and making them more capable of adapting the amount of compute they put onto the difficulty of the task, and this can be agent-solved somehow. So it's definitely an avenue of research that we're exploring.

items.question: How do you think about the work needed to make Mistral's model-serving platform cost-efficient?
items.object: Efficient model serving and Mistral's platform
items.answer: We know that hosting models isn't easy. We know there's a lot of work to be done on the inference side to make serving efficient. There's a lot of work to be done on the training side, because you do need to come up with architectures that are memory-efficient, for instance. That's what Mistral 7B is good at, because it has this sliding-window attention mechanism that makes it more memory-efficient. That's some work that you can do on the training side, but in order to reap all the benefits of a good model, you do need to work a lot on the inference part. We are actively working on that part to make it as efficient as possible, to build a platform that will be very cost-efficient. So you do need to have a good platform with good code, good inference code.

items.question: Why do you think a globally important AI company can emerge from Europe?
items.object: Europe's potential to build a globally important AI company
items.answer: I think some very strong point of Europe on that domain is talent. As it turns out, France, the UK, and Poland are very good at training mathematicians, and as it turns out mathematicians are very good at making AI. So that means that there's a lot of French people, English people, and Polish people in AI, and many of them want to stay in Europe. Their family is there. The food is better. You have many advantages; I can't list them, it would be too long. And so obviously we've been seeing the emergence of an AI ecosystem in London, I think very much thanks to DeepMind, and then in Paris also thanks to DeepMind and to Meta that settled a lab there, and to a lot of entrepreneurs that started to come back. So today we have, I think, hundreds of startups in Paris. This is not the level of Silicon Valley, obviously, but we start to have an ecosystem in place with investors, with operators investing as well. It's the same kind of flywheel that made San Francisco and the Bay Area successes, starting to spin in France, and I'm very glad that we're participating in it.
